answers.text: Same idea as before, fixed three lines every time, same order: delivery date, item and quantity, then any change from the original order. If the email does not mention any change at all, I would have it write 'no change' rather than leave that line blank or skip it. That way the output is always three lines no matter what is in the email.
Same as the memo before, fixed layout works best, date, amount, category, submitter, in that order every time.

It is the dates again for me, not the price, the money side, 100 times 48.50, is right. Something about the 14th, the 19th, and 'three days out' does not sit together properly, I am pretty sure that is where the mistake actually is.

62 from 54 still checks out as about right. But three late out of 62, that is closer to 95%, not the 97% they have written, so that line is wrong. I did not manage to work out if anything is off with the stock number though, that part still reads fine to me.
I would sign off Output 2, since it actually shows the 612,000 and 25,100 behind the 4.1%. Output 1 is just the answer with nothing to check it against.

Reply 2 for me, it has the order number and the credit reference in it so both can be looked up. With reply 1 there is no way to tell if that 10% credit is even real from the sentence alone. It is not that reply 1 is necessarily wrong, I just would not send it as it is.
1. No, personal address, not comfortable pasting that in. 2. Yes. 3. No, not released yet. 4. Yes, already public anyway. 5. No.

The pricing and discount figures I would be careful with, would not paste those in without checking the tool first. The confidentiality clause too, since it names both companies, that is not something I want sitting in a tool we do not control. The delivery schedule on its own is probably fine to include, that is not really sensitive by itself.
I would still want to pull the delivery total and late count myself from the warehouse system before it goes to the manager on Friday, rather than trust the draft as it is.

Step 1 is where trouble starts if the AI reads the order wrong, but the real risk is step 4, since once that confirmation goes out automatically there is no pulling it back. I would flag anything where stock is right at the edge, or the order quantity looks unusually big, and stop it going out automatically in those cases.
